title: The Big Bang
description: The observable universe begins expanding from an extremely hot, dense state. Its age is worked out by fitting the standard cosmological model to the Planck satellite's map of the cosmic microwave background.
uncertainty: The Planck 2018 result is 13.787 billion years, give or take 0.020 billion, and it assumes the standard model of cosmology; what, if anything, came before is unknown.

title: Cosmic inflation
date: 13.8 billion years ago (first fraction of a second)
description: Space is thought to have expanded enormously, faster than light, for a tiny fraction of a second. The idea explains why the universe looks so uniform and flat, and its predictions match the pattern of small ripples seen in the cosmic microwave background.
uncertainty: Inflation is a widely used theory, not a directly observed event; its timing (often put at about 10^-36 to 10^-32 seconds) and cause are not established.

title: First atomic nuclei form
description: In the minutes after the Big Bang, protons and neutrons fused into the nuclei of the lightest elements: hydrogen, helium and traces of lithium and beryllium. After about five minutes most of today's helium existed and the universe had cooled too much for fusion to continue.
uncertainty: The timing comes from well-tested nuclear physics and matches measured hydrogen and helium abundances; sources give the end of fusion as anywhere from about 5 to 20 minutes.

title: First atoms and the cosmic microwave background
date: 13.8 billion years ago (380,000 years after the Big Bang)
description: The universe cooled to about 3,000 kelvin, cool enough for electrons and nuclei to join into neutral atoms, and light could travel freely for the first time. That light is still detectable as the cosmic microwave background, first found in 1964 and mapped in detail by the COBE, WMAP and Planck satellites.
uncertainty: This was a gradual change, not an instant; sources quote about 370,000 to 380,000 years after the Big Bang.

title: The cosmic dark ages
description: After the first atoms formed there were no stars or galaxies, only slowly clumping hydrogen and helium gas. This period lasted roughly 200 million years, until the first stars lit up.
uncertainty: The dark ages have not been observed directly; their length depends on when the first stars formed, which is itself uncertain by 100 million years or more.

title: The first stars
description: Clouds of hydrogen and helium collapsed under gravity to form the first stars, some 200 to 400 million years after the Big Bang. These stars made the first elements heavier than lithium.
uncertainty: No first-generation star has been seen directly; the timing is a model estimate, and galaxies observed 280 million years after the Big Bang show that some stars formed earlier than that.

title: Reionization
description: Ultraviolet light from the first stars and galaxies stripped the electrons from the hydrogen gas between galaxies, turning it from neutral back to ionized. It ran from the end of the dark ages until the universe was about a billion years old, and is traced through the spectra of distant quasars and the polarization of the cosmic microwave background.
uncertainty: The start and end are gradual and debated; Planck data put the midpoint at a redshift of about 7.7, give or take 0.8.

title: Earliest confirmed galaxies
description: The most distant galaxy with a distance confirmed by its spectrum, MoM-z14, is seen as it was about 280 million years after the Big Bang (redshift 14.44). It was measured with the James Webb Space Telescope in 2025, a year after two galaxies were confirmed at about 300 million years.
uncertainty: This is the earliest galaxy confirmed so far, not the first to form; the record has moved several times since 2022 and bright galaxies this early are far more common than models predicted.

title: An early galaxy cluster in the making
description: Seven galaxies packed closely together are seen 650 million years after the Big Bang (redshift 7.88), confirmed by James Webb Space Telescope spectra. The group is expected to grow into a cluster as massive as the largest ones nearby.
uncertainty: It was the most distant confirmed protocluster when reported in 2023, and may since have been surpassed; its future mass is a model extrapolation.

title: Early supermassive black holes
description: The quasar J0313-1806 is seen about 670 million years after the Big Bang (redshift 7.642), powered by a black hole of about 1.6 billion solar masses. It shows that supermassive black holes had already grown very large within the first billion years.
uncertainty: It was the most distant quasar known when reported in 2021; fainter feeding black holes have since been reported even earlier, such as in the galaxy GN-z11 at redshift 10.6, and how they grew so fast is unresolved.

title: The Milky Way's disk begins to form
description: The Milky Way's old, thick disk of stars started forming about 13 billion years ago, only 0.8 billion years after the Big Bang. The date comes from precise ages measured for a large sample of subgiant stars.
uncertainty: A 2022 result that rests on stellar models; individual star ages at this epoch are uncertain by several hundred million years or more.

title: The ancient core of the Milky Way
description: A dense population of very old, metal-poor stars around the galactic centre, with a mass of at least 50 million Suns, appears to be the remains of the early Milky Way before its disk settled. It was identified in 2022.
uncertainty: The stars are not dated individually; their age is inferred from their chemistry and from predating the oldest disk stars, which this study puts at about 12.5 billion years and another puts at about 13 billion.

title: Globular clusters of the Milky Way form
description: The Milky Way's globular clusters, dense balls of hundreds of thousands of old stars, formed over this span. A study of 55 clusters found average ages of about 12.5 billion years for the most metal-poor and about 11 billion years for the metal-rich ones.
uncertainty: Cluster ages carry an overall uncertainty of roughly 1.5 to 2 billion years from distances and chemical abundances.

title: One of the oldest known stars forms: HD 140283
description: HD 140283, a nearby star with very few heavy elements, is among the oldest stars with a measured age. A 2021 study using its measured size and models of how stars age put it at about 12 billion years.
uncertainty: The 2021 figure is 12 billion years, give or take 0.5; a 2013 estimate was 14.46 billion, give or take 0.8, nominally older than the universe, so single-star ages this old remain imprecise.

title: Peak of cosmic star formation
description: The rate at which the universe as a whole formed stars peaked about 3.5 billion years after the Big Bang (redshift about 1.9), a time often called cosmic noon, and has fallen steadily since. This comes from surveys counting ultraviolet and infrared light from galaxies at many distances.
uncertainty: The peak is broad, spanning roughly redshift 1 to 3, and the exact figure depends on corrections for dust.

title: Gaia-Sausage-Enceladus merger
description: The young Milky Way collided with and absorbed a smaller galaxy, about a quarter of its own mass, in its last major merger. The debris makes up much of the inner stellar halo and was recognised in 2018 from the motions and chemistry of stars measured by the Gaia satellite.
uncertainty: Studies disagree on the date: about 10 billion years ago in the 2018 discovery paper cited here, about 11 billion in a 2022 stellar-age study, and 8 to 10 billion in ESA summaries.

title: The Milky Way's central bar forms
description: The elongated bar of stars across the centre of the Milky Way formed and channelled gas inward, setting off a burst of star formation in a small central disk. The oldest stars of that disk, dated with pulsating Mira variable stars, are about 8 billion years old.
uncertainty: The 2024 study gives 8 billion years, give or take 1, as a minimum age for the bar; earlier and much later dates have also been proposed.

title: The Milky Way's thin disk takes shape
description: After its early mergers, the Milky Way entered a calmer phase and steadily built the thin disk of stars and gas where most of its stars, including the Sun, now lie. Stellar ages and chemistry split cleanly into an earlier and a later population at about 8 billion years.
uncertainty: The change was gradual and the two disks overlap in age; an independent estimate from radioactive dating of stars gives 8.8 billion years, give or take 1.7.

title: Expansion of the universe begins to speed up
description: Until then gravity had been slowing the expansion of the universe; as matter thinned out, the outward push of dark energy overcame that braking and the expansion began to accelerate. The acceleration was discovered in 1998 from distant supernovae that appeared fainter than expected.
uncertainty: Sources disagree: about 6 billion years ago here, roughly 5 billion in others, and one NASA page implies under 5 billion; measurements put the changeover at a redshift of roughly 0.5 to 0.6, and the nature of dark energy is unknown.

title: First passage of the Sagittarius dwarf galaxy
description: The small Sagittarius galaxy is thought to have made its first close pass through the Milky Way's disk, and star formation in the Sun's wider neighbourhood rose to a peak 5.7 billion years ago. The burst was found in Gaia measurements of nearby stars.
uncertainty: The burst of star formation is measured, but its link to Sagittarius rests on orbit models that put the passage five to six billion years ago; other ESA material gives four to five.
